content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued a recommendation regarding the duration of bladder catheterization following the surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula. This guideline is intended to provide evidence-based recommendations to improve the health and well-being of women affected by this condition. Obstetric fistula is an abnormal opening between a woman’s genital tract and her urinary tract and/or rectum, typically caused by prolonged obstructed labor. This condition can have devastating consequences for women, including incontinence and social isolation. The WHO recommends a shorter duration of bladder catheterization, specifically 7 to 10 days, as an alternative to longer periods of catheter use after the surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula. This recommendation is based on evidence suggesting that shorter catheterization periods are effective in promoting complete healing while improving patient comfort and potentially reducing the risk of catheter-related urinary tract infections. Additionally, shorter catheterization durations may decrease the need for intensive nursing care, reduce costs, and allow for shorter hospital stays, which is particularly beneficial in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) where healthcare resources are limited. The guideline defines a simple obstetric fistula as a mid-anterior vaginal wall fistula with minimal scarring and a diameter of 3 cm or less. For more complex cases, alternative management strategies may be required. The recommendation is applicable in any context where women experience simple obstetric urinary fistula due to obstructed labor. The development of this guideline followed a rigorous process, including the identification of priority questions, systematic evidence retrieval, and assessment using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology. An international group of experts, known as the Guideline Development Group (GDG), reviewed the evidence and formulated the recommendation. The GDG also considered the balance of benefits and harms, stakeholder values and preferences, and resource implications. The primary audience for this guideline includes healthcare professionals, particularly fistula surgeons and nurses providing postoperative care, as well as policymakers and organizations involved in fistula care services. The guideline aims to standardize care practices, improve patient outcomes, and address the significant burden of obstetric fistula in LMICs. The WHO emphasizes that this recommendation will be regularly reviewed and updated as new evidence becomes available. The organization welcomes suggestions for additional questions to be addressed in future updates. This guideline represents an important step in supporting evidence-informed policies and practices to alleviate the suffering of women with obstetric fistula.
